title: Food and the code
hookLine: the code forbids ritually slaughtered meat; many Sikhs are vegetarian, others not

cards: Two Sikh households, same street, same gurdwara. In one kitchen there hasn't been meat for as long as anyone can remember; the grandmother says it simply isn't their way.
In the other, there's chicken on the stove for dinner. On Sunday morning both families sit side by side in the langar hall and eat the same meal: dal, a vegetable dish, roti and a sweet.
Nobody at the table asks what's waiting at home. What does the Sikh code actually say about food? Less than some expect, and the little it says matters.

teach.b: First, the line it draws. Among the things an initiated Sikh must never do, which you met early on this path, the code names eating kutha: meat from an animal killed by ritual slaughter.
Sikhs explain it in more than one way. Some see it as refusing to take part in another community's rite; others, as one piece of the Sikh refusal of empty ritual. Either way, it's a firm line.
Second, what the code leaves open. It doesn't say every Sikh must be vegetarian, so Sikhs differ.

teach.h: VEGETARIAN, OR NOT: BOTH KEEP THE CODE.
teach.b: Some keep a vegetarian kitchen, and some groups within the panth hold to it strictly and with deep feeling. Others eat meat that isn't kutha. Both families on that street can be keeping the code.

The langar serves vegetarian food so that anyone, whatever their own rules about food, can sit and share it. The Guru's kitchen chooses the meal that leaves no one out. Fourth, the Guru Granth Sahib itself.
In a hymn of Guru Nanak at Ang twelve eighty-nine, the Guru says, in paraphrase, that fools argue about flesh and meat while knowing nothing of meditation and spiritual wisdom.
Some readers take it as a warning not to make food the measure of holiness; others read it alongside their own vegetarian practice and find no conflict.

teach.h: FROM THE PLATE TO THE HEART.
teach.b: The code draws one line about what goes on the plate.
The hymn asks about the one eating.

how: Initiated Sikhs do not eat kutha, ritually slaughtered meat; some Sikhs are vegetarian and others eat other meat, and gurdwara langar is served vegetarian so that everyone can share it.

a rule that every meal be eaten in the gurdwara
the code forbids kutha and leaves vegetarianism open

games.q: you're cooking for the langar, for anyone who walks in the door. what goes in the pot?
o: a meat curry; most people like it.
a vegetarian meal: dal, vegetables, roti.
whatever your own family eats at home.
games.why: the langar serves vegetarian food, so that no one, whatever their own rules, has to stay away from the Guru's table.

practice: If you have something to eat or drink nearby, even a sip of water, look at it first and think of the hands it passed through: a farmer, a driver, a cook.
Then take one small bite or sip, slowly, and notice the taste, the texture, the warmth or the cool. If you pray, remember the Giver as you eat.

wordCard.voice: Food and the code. The code forbids kutha, ritually slaughtered meat, and leaves vegetarianism open; some Sikhs are vegetarian, others are not, and the langar is meatless so all can share. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: meat from ritual slaughter, which the code forbids.

carryVoice: Your line: eat mindfully. One firm line, and a wide table that leaves no one out. That's today, done.
